archetype.name: Playoff Team (ball-control, pass-defense first)
archetype.definition: A Chicago team whose 3-1 record rests on top-five net efficiency, a pass defense that smothers the short game and a clock-eating offense. Unlike last year's 11-win team, which leaned on turnovers, this one is winning on play quality.

report.headline: Real efficiency, not last year's turnover luck, even with Williams sidelined
report.take:
Last year's 11-6 Bears were a mirage in the best sense. They ranked 14th in net EPA and 21st in defensive EPA, and their record came from a league-best +1.3 turnover margin per game and 2.82 wins over expectation. This year's 3-1 is built differently. Net EPA sits at 0.182 (4th) and the point differential at +11.8 per game (3rd). The turnover margin is slightly negative, and the only one-score game they played, a 9-3 loss to Minnesota, went against them. That is a team whose record trails nothing and whose underlying play carries the load.

The engine is a pass defense that looks nothing like last year's. Chicago allows -0.096 EPA per dropback (2nd) and an absurd -0.253 on short throws (2nd), and it converts a 27.6% pressure rate (3rd) into a sack on 8.6% of dropbacks. Opponents are converting just 23.7% on third down. On offense the Bears lead the league in yards per game (430.3) and time of possession (36.6 minutes) while running more than expected. The passing game has been the efficient part at 0.264 EPA per play (6th). The obvious caveat on the defense is the schedule. After Carolina's 9th-ranked offense hung 37 and 361 passing yards in Week 1, the next three opponents rank 28th, 29th and 13th on offense, and Chicago allowed 9, 7 and 12.

The numbers also hide some soft spots. The rushing volume flatters the ground game: 232 yards against the Jets still produced -6.6 rush EPA, and rush EPA has been negative in every game since the opener. The defense that kills the short game bleeds deep (28th in deep EPA, 22nd in explosive pass rate) and is soft against the run (28th). Those weaknesses haven't been punished because the recent opponents couldn't exploit them. The line allows pressure on 20% of dropbacks (26th), and starting tackle Braxton Jones (65% of snaps) is now on IR.

The most encouraging data point is that the offense didn't fall apart without Caleb Williams. With Case Keenum starting Weeks 3 and 4 (Tyson Bagent also logged 322 passing yards), Chicago posted +7.3 and +7.9 pass EPA and scored 27 and 23 points. Williams (hamstring) is listed out with a return estimate after this week, so the trip to Green Bay is another backup game. A well-coached, ball-control team can survive that against a 30th-ranked net-EPA opponent. The full verdict waits on how the defense handles the stretch of Seattle, Detroit, Jacksonville and Buffalo offenses.

strengths.title: Pass defense that erases the short game
strengths.body: Chicago is 2nd in pass EPA allowed and 2nd on short throws, backed by the 3rd-best pressure rate. The rush is getting home without the coverage giving up easy completions, and that drives the 2nd-ranked third-down defense. The pressure component tends to be sticky. The coverage numbers were mostly built against weak offenses, so expect some give with three corners and safeties on the injury report.

strengths.title: Efficiency over luck this time
strengths.body: Last season's record leaned on the league's best turnover margin and nearly three wins over expectation. This year the net EPA is far higher and the turnover margin is slightly negative, so the record isn't propped up by takeaways or close-game breaks. That is the more repeatable kind of 3-1.

strengths.title: Offense holds up with backups
strengths.body: The passing game stayed positive with Keenum, at +7.3 and +7.9 EPA in his two starts, and the offense still leads the league in yards and possession time. The run-leaning, ball-control structure under Ben Johnson shortens games and protects a backup quarterback, which makes the floor without Williams higher than usual.

concerns.title: Deep shots and the run game
concerns.body: The flip side of a defense that suffocates the short game is a 28th-ranked deep EPA allowed and 28th-ranked rush EPA allowed. Carolina's 361 passing yards in Week 1 showed what happens when an offense can attack downfield. With Cam Lewis out and the secondary thinned, this is the most likely point of regression once the schedule brings better offenses.

concerns.title: Rushing volume without value
concerns.body: Chicago runs a lot and gains yards (4.75 per carry, 5th), but rush EPA has been negative in every game since the opener, including -6.6 on 232 yards against the Jets. The ground game is a clock tool more than a scoring one. That matters more while a backup quarterback is under center, and it puts pressure on Kyle Monangai (thumb, questionable) and D'Andre Swift to avoid negative plays.

concerns.title: Leaky protection, now minus a tackle
concerns.body: The line allows pressure on 20% of dropbacks (26th), even if the sack rate is middling. Braxton Jones's move to IR removes a regular starter. A backup quarterback behind a line that leaks pressure is the clearest way this offense stalls.

trend.note: The 59-37 opener is the outlier on both sides of the ball. Since then the defense has allowed 9, 7 and 12 while giving up fewer passing yards each week. The offense has been consistently efficient through the air with Keenum, if unspectacular on the scoreboard.

nextGame.headline: Banged-up, flag-prone Packers line meets Chicago's pass rush
nextGame.body:
Green Bay has been one of the league's worst teams by the numbers: 30th in net EPA, -8 points per game, and 0-4 against the spread, with both wins by one score. Its offense can't run (32nd in rush EPA, 31st in stuff rate allowed). That neutralizes Chicago's biggest defensive hole and pushes the game onto Jordan Love's arm behind a line that has allowed the most QB hits in the league. Love does get the ball out fast (2.479 seconds, 31st), which blunts the rush somewhat. Quick throws also feed directly into Chicago's best trait, its short-pass defense. On the other side, the Packers' defense keeps the ball in front (4th in explosive pass rate allowed) but breaks on third down (29th) and in the red zone (32nd). That is a good setup for a methodical, run-leaning Bears offense.

Availability tilts toward Chicago despite Williams's absence. Green Bay is without center Jacob Monk (96% of snaps) and guard Aaron Banks, with tackle Zach Bako-Bewele on IR. That is a lot of interior turnover for a line already near the bottom of the league. The defense lost linebacker Edgerrin Cooper (83%) for the season, Micah Parsons remains out, and cornerback Brandon Cisse is questionable. For Chicago, the backup-quarterback question is known after two starts. The bigger worries are the secondary, with Cam Lewis out, Kyler Gordon listed out despite a full-participant note, and Anthony Johnson Jr. out, plus Monangai's thumb.

keyMatchups.title: Bears rush vs. depleted Packers interior
keyMatchups.body: Green Bay has allowed 33 QB hits (32nd), and now loses its starting center and a guard. Chicago's 3rd-ranked pressure rate should find a weak point inside. The counter is Love's quick release, so the sacks may come on the occasional longer-developing play rather than every down.

keyMatchups.title: Chicago drives vs. GB red zone
keyMatchups.body: The Packers allow touchdowns on 85.7% of red-zone trips and 48.2% of third downs. A long-possession Bears offense is built to test exactly that. If Keenum keeps drives alive, Chicago's possession edge (36.6 minutes versus Green Bay's 26.8) should widen.

keyMatchups.title: GB run game can't punish weakness
keyMatchups.body: Chicago's 28th-ranked run defense would be a problem against most teams. Green Bay's rushing attack, though, is last in EPA and 30th in yards per carry. The Packers' best path is a deep shot against a thinned Bears secondary, not the ground game.

nextGame.watch: Whether Green Bay, short its center and two corners' worth of certainty on the Chicago side, can hit enough deep balls against the Bears' banged-up secondary to escape a game it otherwise can't control on the ground or on the clock.

restOfSeason.body:
The base is real. A top-five net EPA without help from turnovers or close games is a more trustworthy foundation than last year's 11 wins, and Williams's estimated return after this week restores the offense's ceiling. Expect the defense to come back toward the pack, though. The third-down and short-pass numbers were posted mostly against bottom-tier offenses, and the deep-ball and run-defense holes will face Detroit's 6th-ranked offense twice, Jacksonville's 7th, Buffalo's 3rd and Seattle's 12th. The schedule also offers soft defenses to exploit (Detroit 32nd, Buffalo 29th, Miami 28th, New Orleans 30th), so the offense should hold its scoring pace.

In the division, Minnesota is the hurdle. It is 4-0 with the top-ranked defense and already beat Chicago once, and the Week 18 trip there may decide the North. Points allowed should drift up from 16.3 toward 20. The offense in the 24-28 range, plus a run-heavy approach that limits game variance, points to a double-digit-win season and a playoff berth more likely than not.
swingFactors: Williams's hamstring timeline and how sharp he returns
Secondary health (Lewis, Gordon, Johnson) against the deep ball
Splitting the two late Detroit games and the Week 18 trip to Minnesota

bets.reason: The efficiency gap is wide: Chicago is 4th and Green Bay 30th in net EPA, and the Packers are 0-4 against the spread with a -8 per-game point differential. Chicago covered both backup-quarterback starts. A three-point line on the road treats the Williams absence as more costly than it has looked. Green Bay's line injuries and a seven-point possession-time gap add to the case.

Chicago's last three games finished at 12, 34 and 35 total points, all unders, and its run-leaning, clock-heavy style (1st in possession time) shortens games. Green Bay scores 18.3 a game with the worst rushing offense in the league and is down two interior linemen.

The total and spread imply roughly 21 points for Green Bay, above its 18.3 per-game average. The Packers face a defense allowing 16.3 per game with a 3rd-ranked pressure rate, while their line allows the most QB hits in the league and is missing its center. The main risk is a deep shot against a thin Bears secondary.

confidence.note: Four-game sample with a QB change and a soft middle of the schedule. The efficiency edge is large, but the defense hasn't been tested by good offenses since Week 1.
